growth_story.headline: The UAE economy keeps growing as workers arrive, but income per person is still 64.5 percent below its 1980 peak and lower than in 1970.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in the United Arab Emirates peaked in 1980 and in 2024 was still 64.5 percent below that peak, and lower than in 1970, the first year of the record. From 1990 to 1997 it held roughly steady, growing 0.5 percent a year. From 1998 to 2009 it fell 2.9 percent a year: the IMF describes a Dubai-led push into logistics, tourism and property, in a city whose people were mostly expatriates, that broke in 2009 when the global recession and the bursting of the Dubai property bubble hit together, and income per person fell 11.0 percent that year. Since 2010 it has been almost flat, at -0.1 percent a year, with falls of 4.2 percent in 2017 after the oil price slump and 8.3 percent in 2020, the COVID-19 year. The sources credit expanding non-oil sectors such as tourism, construction, finance and real estate for strong GDP growth, and the IMF finds that added labor was one of the two largest sources of that growth, while income per person averaged -0.8 percent a year over 2016–2024.

threads.title: Hub and property boom
threads.text: In the 2000s Dubai built a second engine beside oil: logistics, business services, tourism and property, opened to foreign buyers around 2004. Most of Dubai's people were expatriates. Income per person fell 2.9 percent a year over 1998–2009.

threads.text: When oil prices fell, the government cut spending, and the IMF reports that this cutback slowed non-oil growth and hurt banks. Income per person fell 4.2 percent in 2017, one of the dips in an otherwise flat era since 2010.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a strong, broad-based economy with fast GDP growth and booming non-oil sectors, both now and in the 2000s. The data on income per person do not show that: it fell 2.9 percent a year over 1998–2009, has averaged -0.1 percent a year since 2010, and fell 0.8 percent in 2024. Part of the gap is the growing number of people: the IMF counts more labor among the largest sources of non-oil growth, and output per person has not kept pace. The sources rarely talk about income per person.
